questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: At no point did the CEO deny the allegations.
At no point the CEO denied the allegations.
At no point the CEO did deny the allegations.
At no point deny did the CEO the allegations.
questions.explanation: 'At no point' triggers inversion: 'did the CEO deny the allegations.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The regulator requires that all banks maintain a minimum capital reserve.
The regulator requires that all banks maintains a minimum capital reserve.
The regulator requires that all banks will maintain a minimum capital reserve.
The regulator requires that all banks maintaining a minimum capital reserve.
questions.explanation: After 'require that', formal English uses the subjunctive: 'all banks maintain a minimum reserve.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If only the board had acted sooner, the losses could have been minimized.
If only the board acted sooner, the losses could have been minimized.
If only the board had act sooner, the losses could have been minimized.
If only the board had acted sooner, the losses will have been minimized.
questions.explanation: 'If only' + past perfect expresses regret about the past: 'If only the board had acted sooner...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The results were mixed. That being said, the outlook remains positive.
The results were mixed, that being said the outlook remains positive.
The results were mixed. That being said the outlook remains positive.
The results were mixed that being said, the outlook remains positive.
questions.explanation: 'That being said' begins a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'That being said, the outlook remains positive.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: It was only when sales dropped that management took notice.
It was only when sales dropped when management took notice.
It only was when sales dropped that management took notice.
It was only when sales dropping that management took notice.
questions.explanation: The cleft 'It was only when...that' emphasizes a turning point: 'It was only when sales dropped that management took notice.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Analysts speculate that the central bank will cut rates again.
Analysts speculate to that the central bank will cut rates again.
Analysts speculate the central bank cutting rates again that.
Analysts are speculate that the central bank will cut rates again.
questions.explanation: 'Speculate' is followed by 'that + clause': 'speculate that the central bank will cut rates.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Assuming that costs remain stable, margins should improve next year.
Assume that costs remain stable, margins should improve next year.
Assumed that costs remain stable, margins should improve next year.
Assuming costs remaining stable, margins should improve next year.
questions.explanation: 'Assuming that' introduces a conditional assumption: 'Assuming that costs remain stable, margins should improve.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The bulk of the revenue comes from overseas markets.
The bulk of the revenue come from overseas markets.
The bulk of the revenue coming from overseas markets.
A bulk the revenue comes from overseas markets.
questions.explanation: 'The bulk of' + uncountable noun takes a singular verb: 'the bulk of the revenue comes from overseas markets.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The team needn't have rushed the launch; the deadline was later extended.
The team needn't rushed the launch; the deadline was later extended.
The team didn't need have rushed the launch; the deadline was later extended.
The team needn't have rushing the launch; the deadline was later extended.
questions.explanation: 'Needn't have + past participle' expresses an unnecessary past action: 'needn't have rushed the launch.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The reform will not merely cut costs but also improve efficiency.
The reform will not merely cut costs but also improving efficiency.
The reform not merely will cut costs but also improve efficiency.
The reform will not merely cutting costs but also improve efficiency.
questions.explanation: 'Not merely...but also' links two parallel verb phrases: 'will not merely cut costs but also improve efficiency.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The seemingly minor error caused significant delays.
The seeming minor error caused significant delays.
The error seemingly minor it caused significant delays.
The error caused seemingly minor significant delays.
questions.explanation: 'Seemingly' hedges a description before an adjective: 'the seemingly minor error.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Rates may rise further, in which case borrowing costs will increase.
Rates may rise further, in that case which borrowing costs will increase.
Rates may rise further, which case borrowing costs will increase.
Rates may rise further, in which borrowing costs will increase case.
questions.explanation: 'In which case' refers back to a stated possibility: 'Rates may rise further, in which case borrowing costs will increase.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: So great was the demand that the company doubled production.
So great the demand was that the company doubled production.
So great was the demand the company doubled production.
So great was that the demand the company doubled production.
questions.explanation: Fronting 'so + adjective' triggers inversion: 'So great was the demand that the company doubled production.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The reduction in headcount was announced without warning.
The reduce in headcount was announced without warning.
The reduction in headcount were announced without warning.
The reducing headcount was announced without warning.
questions.explanation: Formal writing nominalizes verbs: 'reduce' becomes 'the reduction in...'

questions.topic: Passive with modal perfect (need not have been)
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The delay need not have been so costly.
The delay need not been so costly.
The delay need not have been so cost.
The delay need not have being so costly.
questions.explanation: Modal perfect passive: 'need not have been + adjective/participle': 'need not have been so costly.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: One team met the target; the other, fell short.
One team met the target; the other met, fell short.
One team met the target; the other is fell short.
One team met the target; the other falls short already.
questions.explanation: Ellipsis omits the repeated verb after a semicolon: 'the other, fell short' (= the other team fell short).

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Costs rose. This, in turn, pushed up retail prices.
Costs rose, this in turn pushed up retail prices.
Costs rose. This in turn pushed up retail prices.
Costs rose this, in turn pushed up retail prices.
questions.explanation: 'In turn' is set off by commas mid-sentence: 'This, in turn, pushed up retail prices.'

questions.topic: Concession connectors (be that as it may)
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The costs are high. Be that as it may, the investment is worthwhile.
The costs are high, be that as it may the investment is worthwhile.
The costs are high. Be that as it may the investment is worthwhile.
The costs are high be that as it may, the investment is worthwhile.
questions.explanation: 'Be that as it may' is a fixed formal concessive phrase and begins a new sentence with a comma.

questions.question: Which is the most appropriate formal opening line for an email introducing yourself to a new business contact?
options: Hi, it's me, we should totally connect sometime.
I am writing to introduce myself as the new account manager for your region.
Yo, new account manager here, let's chat.
Hey there, just wanted to say hi and introduce myself.
questions.explanation: 'I am writing to introduce myself as...' is a standard formal introduction opening.

questions.question: Which is the most appropriate opening line for a formal complaint about a missed deadline by a contractor?
options: I am writing to express concern over the failure to meet the agreed deadline.
You missed the deadline and that's not okay.
I am writing to express concern over the failure to meet the agreed deadline, seriously.
The deadline was missed, which is honestly pretty annoying.
questions.explanation: Formal complaints use precise, measured language such as 'I am writing to express concern over...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The board needs to weigh up the risks before proceeding.
The board needs to weigh the risks up of before proceeding.
The board needs to weigh up of the risks before proceeding.
The board needs to weigh the risks of up before proceeding.
questions.explanation: 'Weigh up' means 'to carefully consider': 'weigh up the risks before proceeding.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The industry has seen its profit margins squeezed by rising costs.
The industry has seen its profit margins squeeze by rising costs.
The industry has seen squeezed its profit margins by rising costs.
The industry has seen its profit margins squeezing by rising costs.
questions.explanation: 'See + object + past participle' describes an experienced change: 'seen its profit margins squeezed.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: All told, the quarter was a modest success.
All telling, the quarter was a modest success.
All tell, the quarter was a modest success.
All told that, the quarter was a modest success.
questions.explanation: 'All told' is a fixed absolute participle phrase meaning 'in total, overall.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The flight was delayed on account of adverse weather.
The flight was delayed on the account of adverse weather.
The flight was delayed account of adverse weather.
The flight was delayed on account for adverse weather.
questions.explanation: 'On account of' means 'because of': 'delayed on account of adverse weather.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Small suppliers bore the brunt of the price war.
Small suppliers carried the brunt of the price war.
Small suppliers bore of the brunt of the price war.
Small suppliers took the brunt bore of the price war.
questions.explanation: 'Bear the brunt' is a fixed collocation: 'small suppliers bore the brunt of the price war.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The startup has steadily built a loyal customer base.
The startup has built steadily a loyal customer base.
Steadily the startup has built a loyal customer base.
The startup steadily has built a loyal customer base.
questions.explanation: Adverbs of manner typically follow the auxiliary verb: 'has steadily built.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The proposal may be revised. In any event, the deadline stands.
The proposal may be revised, in any event the deadline stands.
The proposal may be revised. In any event the deadline stands.
The proposal may be revised in any event, the deadline stands.
questions.explanation: 'In any event' begins a new sentence and is followed by a comma.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: The directors would seldom overrule the chair, would they?
The directors would seldom overrule the chair, wouldn't they?
The directors would seldom overrule the chair, don't they?
The directors would seldom overrule the chair, do they?
questions.explanation: 'Seldom' makes the statement effectively negative, so the tag is positive: 'would seldom overrule..., would they?'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The audit findings were not entirely surprising.
The audit findings were not all surprising entirely.
The audit findings not were entirely surprising.
The audit findings were entirely not surprising.
questions.explanation: Formal understatement places 'not' before the adverb: 'were not entirely surprising.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Were it to happen again, the fallout would be far worse.
Was it to happen again, the fallout would be far worse.
Were it happen again, the fallout would be far worse.
Were it to happen again, the fallout will be far worse.
questions.explanation: 'Were + subject + to + infinitive' is a formal inverted hypothetical conditional: 'Were it to happen again, the fallout would be far worse.'
